messages.content:
You are Knack's robot programmer. You write a Python skill for a 5-DoF robot arm with a
parallel gripper on a tabletop, then improve it from practice results. Nobody will show you a
demonstration: you learn only from what happens when your code runs.

How practice works
- Your code must define `def run(robot):`. It runs on many randomised layouts of the scene:
  object positions, orientations, masses and friction change every episode. Never hard-code
  coordinates. Read them at run time with robot.observe() or robot.get_pose().
- After each round you get the outcome of every episode, a failure analysis and traces of the
  robot calls your code made. Use them to fix the code. Keep what works.
- Allowed imports: math, numpy, itertools, functools, collections. No file, network or OS access,
  no bare `except:`. Each episode has a simulated-time budget, so no long waits or endless loops.
- Return True if you believe the task succeeded, otherwise False. The return value is logged
  but it is not how success is measured.

Robot API (all units metres / radians, world frame: x forward from the robot base,
y to the robot's left, z up, table surface at z = 0; the base is at x=0, y=0):

robot.observe() -> dict
    Snapshot of the scene from the robot's perception (positions have ~2 mm noise):
    {"time": s,
     "gripper": {"pos": [x, y, z], "yaw": rad, "opening": m, "holding": name or None},
     "objects": {name: {"pos": [x, y, z], "yaw": rad, "shape": "cube"|"puck",
                        "size": [...], "color": str}},
     "fixtures": {name: {"pos": [x, y, 0], "kind": "zone"|"tray", "color": str,
                         "radius": m (zones), "inner_half_size": m, "wall_height": m (trays)}}}
    "pos" of an object is its centre. Cube yaw is reported in [-pi/4, pi/4) (90 deg symmetry).

robot.get_pose(name) -> {"pos": [x, y, z], "yaw": rad}
    Pose of one object or fixture (same noise as observe()).

robot.move_to(x, y, z, yaw=None, speed=None) -> {"ok": bool, "pos": [x, y, z], "error_m": float}
    Move the gripper's tool point (midway along the fingers, between the finger pads) in a
    straight line to (x, y, z). The gripper points straight down when reachable and tilts
    automatically near the edge of the workspace.
    yaw: world angle of the fingers' closing direction. Pass an object's yaw to line the
    fingers up with its faces. None keeps the natural orientation.
    speed: m/s, default 0.15, capped at 0.30 by the safety layer.
    The fingertips reach 1.25 cm below the tool point. A cube resting on the table has its
    centre at z = 0.015, so z = 0.015 puts the finger pads around its middle.
    Raises MotionError (an Exception you may catch) if the target is unreachable.
    "ok" is False if the gripper was blocked before reaching the target.

robot.move_by(dx=0, dy=0, dz=0, speed=None) -> same as move_to, relative to the current tool point.

robot.grasp() -> bool
    Close the fingers (max opening 5 cm). Returns True if an object is held between them.

robot.release() -> None
    Open the fingers fully (5 cm gap).

robot.holding() -> name or None
robot.home() -> None              Move to a safe pose above the table.
robot.wait(seconds) -> None       Let time pass (max 5 s per call).
robot.log(*values) -> None        Write a debug note into the episode trace.

Safety layer (not negotiable): the tool point must stay inside x in [0.04, 0.32],
y in [-0.26, 0.26], z in [0.014, 0.26]. Targets up to 2 cm outside are clamped; further
out halts the skill. Pressing the gripper into the table with more than 30 N halts the
skill. Halts cannot be caught. Each episode has a time budget (simulated seconds).
Reachable band: roughly 0.10-0.23 m horizontal distance from the base at table height,
less when the tool point is high.

Good practice (any task)
- Perceive, act, verify, recover: re-read poses after important actions (for example check
  robot.holding() after robot.grasp()) and retry a bounded number of times if a check fails.
- Catch MotionError around moves that might be out of reach and choose another approach.
- Keep moves near objects slow (speed 0.05-0.10) and travel moves at the default speed.

Reply format (always both parts):
<notes>
3-8 short bullets: what the last results taught you and what you changed. Carry forward
useful facts from earlier notes.
</notes>
```python
# the complete skill module
```

reply:
<notes>
- First version; no practice results yet. Design choices based on the perception note:
- Camera noise ~1 cm per reading → average 6 get_pose() calls per pose; use a 4×-angle circular mean for cube yaw (reported in [-π/4, π/4), wraps at ±45°).
- Don't trust observed z for grasping: cubes rest on the table, so grasp at fixed tool z = 0.015 (pads at cube middle).
- Trays have 2.5 cm walls and 8.8 cm interior → carry cube in low (tool z ≈ 0.028, cube bottom ~1.3 cm above floor) and release inside, avoiding drop-bounce; verify with a fresh averaged reading and retry if it landed outside.
- Verify every step: holding() after grasp, after lift, and after transport (friction/grip force vary → drops possible); re-pick on loss.
- Clamp all move targets just inside the safety box and catch MotionError so a bad layout can't halt the skill; bounded retries everywhere (max 4 pick attempts, 3 full cycles per cube).
- Watch for next round: grasp failures from residual centering error, cubes bouncing off tray walls, and any unreachable-pose MotionErrors.
</notes>
```python
import math


def _clamp(v, lo, hi):
    return max(lo, min(hi, v))


def _avg_pose(robot, name, n=6):
    """Average n noisy readings of a pose; circular mean on 4*yaw to
    handle the cube's 90-degree yaw symmetry / wrap at +-pi/4."""
    sx = sy = sz = 0.0
    s4 = c4 = 0.0
    for _ in range(n):
        p = robot.get_pose(name)
        pos = p["pos"]
        sx += pos[0]
        sy += pos[1]
        sz += pos[2]
        a = 4.0 * float(p.get("yaw", 0.0))
        s4 += math.sin(a)
        c4 += math.cos(a)
    yaw = math.atan2(s4, c4) / 4.0
    return sx / n, sy / n, sz / n, yaw


def _move(robot, x, y, z, yaw=None, speed=None):
    """move_to with targets clamped inside the safety box and
    MotionError caught so nothing can halt the skill."""
    x = _clamp(x, 0.05, 0.31)
    y = _clamp(y, -0.25, 0.25)
    z = _clamp(z, 0.015, 0.25)
    try:
        return robot.move_to(x, y, z, yaw=yaw, speed=speed)
    except Exception as exc:
        robot.log("move error", round(x, 3), round(y, 3), round(z, 3), exc)
        return None


def _pick(robot, name):
    for _ in range(4):
        x, y, _, yaw = _avg_pose(robot, name)
        robot.release()
        if _move(robot, x, y, 0.085, yaw=yaw) is None:
            continue
        if _move(robot, x, y, 0.015, yaw=yaw, speed=0.05) is None:
            _move(robot, x, y, 0.07, speed=0.1)
            continue
        robot.grasp()
        if robot.holding() == name:
            _move(robot, x, y, 0.11, speed=0.08)
            if robot.holding() == name:
                robot.log("picked", name)
                return True
        robot.release()
        _move(robot, x, y, 0.07, speed=0.1)
    robot.log("pick failed", name)
    return False


def _in_tray(robot, cube, tray):
    cx, cy, cz, _ = _avg_pose(robot, cube, n=4)
    tx, ty, _, _ = _avg_pose(robot, tray, n=4)
    dx = cx - tx
    dy = cy - ty
    inside = (dx * dx + dy * dy) < (0.035 * 0.035) and cz < 0.024
    robot.log("in_tray", cube, inside, round(dx, 3), round(dy, 3), round(cz, 3))
    return inside


def _place(robot, cube, tray):
    tx, ty, _, _ = _avg_pose(robot, tray)
    if _move(robot, tx, ty, 0.13) is None:
        return False
    if robot.holding() != cube:
        robot.log("lost in transport", cube)
        return False
    if _move(robot, tx, ty, 0.05, speed=0.08) is None:
        return False
    # lower the held cube into the tray (bottom ~1.3 cm above the floor,
    # below the 2.5 cm wall top) then release: minimal drop, no bounce
    _move(robot, tx, ty, 0.028, speed=0.05)
    robot.release()
    _move(robot, tx, ty, 0.12, speed=0.1)
    return _in_tray(robot, cube, tray)


def run(robot):
    robot.home()
    tasks = (("red_cube", "red_tray"), ("blue_cube", "blue_tray"))
    ok_all = True
    for cube, tray in tasks:
        done = False
        for _ in range(3):
            if _in_tray(robot, cube, tray):
                done = True
                break
            if robot.holding() != cube:
                if not _pick(robot, cube):
                    continue
            if _place(robot, cube, tray):
                done = True
                break
        if not done:
            ok_all = False
            robot.log("FAILED", cube, tray)
    robot.home()
    robot.log("finished, ok_all =", ok_all)
    return ok_all
```
reasoning:
Let me think about this task carefully.

We have a 5-DoF robot arm with a parallel gripper. Task: put red cube into red tray, blue cube into blue tray.

Key facts:
- Object poses from overhead camera, noisy (~1 cm position, several degrees yaw). Every observe() gives fresh noisy reading.
- Mass, friction, grip force vary.
- Trays have walls (wall_height 0.025, inner_half_size 0.044). So we need to drop the cube inside the tray, above the wall height.
- Cubes are 0.03 m, center at z=0.015 when resting.
- Gripper: max opening 5 cm, fingertips reach 1.25 cm below tool point. Tool point z = 0.015 puts finger pads around cube middle.
- Safety: tool point x in [0.04, 0.32], y in [-0.26, 0.26], z in [0.014, 0.26].
- Reachable band: roughly 0.10-0.23 m horizontal distance from base at table height.

Strategy:
1. Observe scene, find red cube, blue cube, red tray, blue tray.
2. For each cube: move above it, align yaw, descend, grasp, verify holding, lift, move above tray center, lower to above wall height, release, verify.
3. Re-observe before each grasp to get fresh pose (averaging multiple observations could help reduce noise).

Since positions are noisy (~1 cm), averaging multiple observe() calls would help. Let me implement a helper that takes N observations and averages positions and yaws (careful with yaw wraparound; cube yaw in [-pi/4, pi/4) with 90-degree symmetry — averaging angles is tricky; could use mean of sin/cos of 4*angle to handle symmetry, or just take a few samples and average with circular mean).

Actually for grasping a 3 cm cube with 5 cm gripper opening, yaw precision of a few degrees doesn't matter much. Position precision matters more: 1 cm error on a 3 cm cube could cause grasp failure. Averaging ~5 observations reduces noise by sqrt(5) ≈ 2.2, so ~4-5 mm. That's good.

Also, the cube might be near a tray wall or in a tray? No — cubes start on the table. Trays are fixtures.

- Get averaged pose of cube.
- Move to pre-grasp: (x, y, z=0.06) with yaw = cube yaw.
- Move down to z=0.015 slowly.
- grasp(), check holding(). If not, retry: re-observe, maybe adjust.
- Lift to z=0.10.

Plan for place:
- Get tray pose (fixtures probably static, but noisy readings — average too).
- Move above tray center at z = wall_height + cube half + margin. Actually when holding the cube, the tool point is at cube middle (z=0.015 when cube on table). The cube is held with pads around its middle, so cube center ≈ tool point z. To drop into tray, we want cube bottom above the wall (0.025) so it clears walls, then release. Tool point z ≈ 0.025 + 0.015 + small margin = ~0.05. Maybe release lower: tool z = 0.04, drop 2.5 cm. Wall height 0.025, cube bottom at tool z - 0.015. At tool z=0.04, cube bottom = 0.025, exactly wall height. Finger width unknown, but the gripper descending into the tray might collide with walls if fingers are wide. The tool point is midway along fingers; fingertips extend 1.25 cm below tool point. When holding a cube at its middle, fingertips are 1.25 cm below cube center, i.e., at cube bottom level (cube half = 1.5 cm... wait fingertips at tool z - 0.0125; cube bottom at tool z - 0.015; so fingertips are 2.5 mm above cube bottom). But with 1 cm perception noise on tray position, centering is uncertain to ~5mm after averaging. Risky but probably OK.

Cubes are light; bounce possible but tray walls contain it. Let's do release at z ≈ 0.055 to be safe clearing walls, then verify with observe that cube is inside tray (within inner_half_size of tray center). If not, retry.

Averaging observations: write helper `avg_pose(name, n=5)` that calls robot.get_pose(name) n times, averages pos, and averages yaw using complex mean of angle*4? Cube yaw reported in [-pi/4, pi/4) due to 90° symmetry. Noise of several degrees won't cross the boundary usually, but near ±pi/4 it could wrap. Use circular mean on 4*yaw then divide by 4 to handle the symmetry robustly. For fixtures, yaw not given (trays presumably axis-aligned; only pos given). get_pose returns yaw too? For fixtures, observe gives pos only... The fixture dict has no yaw. get_pose(name) returns {"pos", "yaw"} — for fixtures maybe yaw=0. We only need tray pos.

Gripper yaw for grasping: pass cube yaw so fingers align with faces. With 5 cm opening and 3 cm cube, even 45° misalignment might still grasp but could push the cube. Aligning is better.

Also note: fresh noisy reading each call — so after moving above the cube, re-observe before final descent? The cube doesn't move (unless we bump it). Best: average pose, move above, then descend. Optionally, do a final corrective: after moving to pre-grasp, take another averaged reading and adjust x,y at low height before descending. But each get_pose has noise; averaging 5 gives ~4.5mm. Descending from 6 cm to 1.5 cm — if our x,y is off by 5mm, the gripper fingers (opening 5cm) might still capture the 3cm cube? Fingertips straddle; if center offset by 5mm, one finger is 5mm from cube face... opening 5 cm, cube 3 cm → 1 cm gap each side when centered. 5 mm offset leaves 5mm gap one side, 15mm other — still fine, grasp() closes fingers and will contact. 2. move_to(x, y, 0.08, yaw=yaw) — pre-grasp high.
3. move_to(x, y, 0.03, yaw=yaw, speed slow) — just above cube... actually descend directly to 0.015? Move to 0.015 with speed 0.05. The safety z min is 0.014; 0.015 is fine.
4. grasp(); if holding: lift to 0.10. Else: lift, re-observe, retry (up to 3 attempts).

2. move_to(tx, ty, 0.12) high above tray.
3. move_to(tx, ty, 0.05, speed slow).
4. Check holding(); if lost, handle (re-pick).

```python
import math

def run(robot):
    try:
        pairs = [("red_cube", "red_tray"), ("blue_cube", "blue_tray")]
        for cube_name, tray_name in pairs:
            success = place_in_tray(robot, cube_name, tray_name)
            if not success:
                # try once more
                success = place_in_tray(robot, cube_name, tray_name)
        # final check
        return check_all(robot)
    except Exception as e:
        robot.log("top-level error", e)

```

But "no bare except" — catch Exception is fine (not bare except). MotionError is an Exception subclass; catching Exception around moves also catches MotionError. But careful not to catch halts — halts can't be caught anyway.

Helper functions:

```python
def avg_pose(robot, name, n=5):
    xs=[]; ys=[]; zs=[]; s4=0.0; c4=0.0
    for _ in range(n):
        p = robot.get_pose(name)
        xs.append(p["pos"][0]); ys.append(p["pos"][1]); zs.append(p["pos"][2])
        a = 4.0*p.get("yaw", 0.0)
        s4 += math.sin(a); c4 += math.cos(a)
    x = sum(xs)/n; y=sum(ys)/n; z=sum(zs)/n
    yaw = math.atan2(s4, c4)/4.0
    return x, y, z, yaw
```

Wait, for fixtures get_pose returns yaw? Spec says get_pose(name) -> {"pos","yaw"} for one object or fixture. OK, yaw exists. For trays we ignore yaw.

Hmm, one concern: does get_pose work for fixtures? "Pose of one object or fixture". Yes.

```python
def pick(robot, name, attempts=4):
    for i in range(attempts):
        x, y, z, yaw = avg_pose(robot, name, 5)
        # approach from above
        try:
            robot.move_to(x, y, 0.09, yaw=yaw)
        except Exception:
            # maybe unreachable; nudge toward base
            ...
        robot.move_to(x, y, 0.016, yaw=yaw, speed=0.05)
        if robot.grasp():
            if robot.holding() == name or robot.holding() is not None:
                robot.move_by(dz=0.09, speed=0.1)
                return True
        # failed: retreat and retry
        robot.move_by(dz=0.06, speed=0.1)
    return False
```

Note: holding() returns name or None. Check it equals the cube name (could accidentally grasp something else? unlikely).

Descend target z: cube center at ~0.015. Use 0.015. Safety min z = 0.014, clamped up to 2cm outside... 0.015 is inside [0.014, 0.26]. Good.

But wait: noisy z from camera? z also noisy ~1cm? "Positions can be off by about a centimetre" — probably mostly x,y from overhead camera; z of an object on the table is known ~0.015. We don't rely on observed z for grasp height anyway; we use fixed 0.015 since cubes rest on the table. Good — that's robust.

It returns {"ok", "pos", "error_m"} — pos is presumably achieved/target pos). Let me just release and verify.

```python
def in_tray(robot, cube_name, tray_name):
    cx, cy, cz, _ = avg_pose(robot, cube_name, 3)
    tx, ty, tz, _ = avg_pose(robot, tray_name, 3)
    dx = cx-tx; dy = cy-ty
    return (dx*dx+dy*dy) < (0.035)**2 and cz < 0.024
```

Use 0.035 (< 0.044 half size) to be safe with noise. cz < 0.024 ensures it's settled inside, not on top of a wall (cube on wall top would be at z ≈ 0.025+0.015=0.04).

Full flow per cube:

```python
def do_one(robot, cube, tray):
    for attempt in range(3):
        if robot.holding() != cube:
            if not pick(robot, cube):
                continue
        if place(robot, cube, tray):
            return True
        # place failed; cube may be somewhere odd; loop re-picks
    return False
```
